## The problem

Modern scientific instruments and simulations produce data that are large, high-dimensional, and noisy. Much of what a scientist wants from such data depends on knowing what they contain, namely which populations or physical regimes are present and what those imply about physics. When no labels exist, that question falls to unsupervised learning, which in turn hands an analyst every degree of freedom a label would otherwise have fixed, such as data resolutions, neighborhood sizes, cluster counts, and model forms. My work builds methods that let the data make those choices.

## The Methods

My methods begin by compressing a large, noisy data set into a small number of representative observations that remain in the units of the data. Pooling observations this way suppresses noise and leaves a representation a scientist can inspect directly, rather than a latent space that has to be decoded. From these representatives the methods learn how the data are organized, which parts of the data space connect to which, and that learned organization is what drives everything downstream, from visualization to clustering.

Three goals run through this work. The first is to make the consequential choices in an unsupervised analysis, such as how finely to resolve the data, how large a neighborhood counts as local, and how many groups are present, into quantities the data determine through explicit statistical criteria rather than settings an analyst tunes. The second is to keep the results in a form a scientist can interpret directly, so that a representative observation can be measured like data and a cluster can be checked against what is known about the system that produced it. The third is to attach evidence to what the methods find, both by separating genuine structure from structured noise and by quantifying the uncertainty of the results, so that a discovery made without labels can still be defended.

## Science from those methods

In simulations of star-forming clouds, prototype embeddings organized thousands of dense gas cores into three evolutionary phases with no knowledge of their fates, and mapping observed cores into the same space predicted that a substantial fraction of cataloged starless cores will never form stars. In the Green Bank Ammonia Survey, MPEC found spatially coherent gas structures from spectral similarity alone, raised the signal-to-noise of faint emission by pooling, and revealed velocity offsets between molecular species that signal gas falling onto the Orion A filament. In the Spitzer Extended Solar Neighborhood Archive, I am building a fully Bayesian census of young stars in which selection effects and missing photometry are modeled rather than cleaned away.

## Where this is going

Physics-informed supervised learning now has a settled vocabulary for where physics enters a model. Its unsupervised counterpart does not exist yet. My long-term program is to build it: methods in which physical constraints shape how structure is discovered without foreclosing the discovery of regimes that existing models do not anticipate, with the statistical accounting to say how much of a result the physics decided.
